question.text: Find the scale factor of the transformation represented by the rotation-scaling matrix $A= \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
The scale factor $r$ of the rotation-scaling matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}$ can be found using the formula \[ r=\sqrt{\det(A)}=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}. \]

Therefore, we obtain \begin{align*} r &= \sqrt{\det(A)} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{(-4)^2+(2)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{16+4} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{20}\\[3pt] &= 2\sqrt{5}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Since $A$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, then we can write \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $r$ is the scale factor and $\theta$ the angle of rotation.

According to the diagram, $r=3$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Therefore, \begin{align} A &= \begin{bmatrix} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

example.title: Constructing a Rotation-Scaling Matrix That Represents a Geometric Transformation

question.text: Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ shown above. Find the vector $A\mathbf{v}$ given that \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a rotation-scaling matrix. So, we need to find its scale factor and the angle of rotation.

We can find the scale factor using the following formula:

\begin{align*} r &= \sqrt{\det(A)} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\right)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{18}+\dfrac{1}{18}} \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{align*}

Now, we can represent $A$ as a product of a rotation and a scaling matrix, as follows:

\begin{align*} A &= \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Hence, we obtain that

\[ \begin{cases} \cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}. \]

Therefore, in order to find $A\mathbf{v}$, we need to rotate $\mathbf{v}$ counterclockwise by an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and scale the result by a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{3},$ as shown below.

example.title: Constructing a Rotation-Scaling Matrix That Represents a Geometric Transformation

question.text: Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ shown above. Find the vector $A\mathbf{v}$ given that \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{3} & -2 \\ 2 & 2\sqrt{3} \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is a rotation-scaling matrix. So, we need to find its scale factor and the angle of rotation.

We can find the scale factor using the following formula:

\begin{align*} r &= \sqrt{\det(A)} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{(2\sqrt{3})^2+(2)^2} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{12+4} \\[3pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

Now, we can represent $A$ as a product of a rotation and a scaling matrix, as follows:

\begin{align*} A &= 4 \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\dfrac12 \\ \dfrac12 & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\dfrac12 \\ \dfrac12 & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Hence, we obtain that

\[ \begin{cases} \cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \sin\theta=\dfrac12 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}. \]

Therefore, in order to find $A\mathbf{v}$, we need to rotate $\mathbf{v}$ counterclockwise by an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and scale the result by a scale factor of $4,$ as shown below.
